reasons: Frontmatter homes lists '[[Third-Party Doctrine & CSLI]]' with role 'Lower-court development (ALPR)', matching the asserted home_role.
The opinion's Section III.A analyzes LPR/ALPR data under Carpenter/Knotts third-party-doctrine and CSLI framing, so the placement and 'ALPR' descriptor are well supported.

Opinion p.1: 'Because the use of an LPR did not constitute a search, no warrant was required; the stop was supported by reasonable suspicion, and the officer found the Glock and its machinegun conversion switch in plain view. Our circuit precedent forecloses Porter's Second Amendment challenge. We affirm.' — matches every clause of the holding.

Section III.A holds LPR use did not invade a reasonable expectation of privacy and was no search; Section III.B.1 holds the stop was supported by reasonable suspicion; III.B.2.a upholds the plain-view seizure of the Glock and switch; Section V holds circuit precedent (Hollis/Wilson) forecloses the § 922(o) Second Amendment challenge; disposition AFFIRMED.
Charge was 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) machinegun possession; conviction affirmed — 'machinegun conviction was affirmed' is accurate.
residual_risks: The firearm was physically retrieved during an inventory search, but the court affirmed on plain view (upholding the district court's plain-view determination), so 'lawfully seized ... in plain view' tracks the court's rationale.
